          "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$. For an integer $r\\ge1$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $B\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region whose boundary is, near each boundary point and in coordinates $y=Qx+c$ for some $Q\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}$ and $c\\in\\mathbb R^3$ with $Q^{\\mathsf T}Q=I_3$, the graph of a $C^1$ function; let $U\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\\overline B\\subset U$. A smooth motion is a map $\\chi:I\\times U\\to\\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ such that, for every $t\\in I$, the map $\\chi_t(a):=\\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open set $\\chi_t(U)$ with a $C^2$ inverse and with $\\det D_a\\chi(t,a)>0$ for all $a\\in U$. The coordinate $a$ labels a reference point and $x=\\chi(t,a)$ is its current position; $\\Omega:=\\{(t,x):t\\in I,\\ x\\in\\chi_t(U)\\}$ is the swept open set and $\\Omega_t:=\\chi_t(B)$ is the current image of $B$.\n\nFor $(t,x)\\in\\Omega$, define the inverse label $A(t,x)$ by $\\chi(t,A(t,x))=x$, and put $F(t,a):=D_a\\chi(t,a)$ and $J(t,a):=\\det F(t,a)$. The joint map $H(t,a):=(t,\\chi(t,a))$ is injective and has block-triangular derivative with determinant $J(t,a)>0$. The Euclidean inverse function theorem therefore gives local $C^1$ inverses; they agree on overlaps because the label is unique, so $A$ is globally $C^1$ on $\\Omega$. Define the Eulerian velocity field $u(t,x):=\\partial_t\\chi(t,A(t,x))$; an Eulerian field is a function of time and current position. Thus $u$ is $C^1$.\n\nFor any $C^1$ scalar or vector field $f$ on $\\Omega$, its material derivative is $D_tf:=\\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$, componentwise; it is the derivative along the curves $t\\mapsto\\chi(t,a)$. Here $D_xf$ and $D_a\\chi$ are the matrices of coordinate partial derivatives. Define the spatial velocity gradient $L:=D_xu$, its symmetric and skew-symmetric parts $D:=(L+L^{\\mathsf T})/2$ and $W:=(L-L^{\\mathsf T})/2$, the scalar $\\theta:=\\operatorname{tr}L=\\sum_{i=1}^3\\partial_{x_i}u_i$, and the trace-free part $D_0:=D-\\theta I_3/3$. The trace is the sum of diagonal entries, and $I_3$ is the $3\\times3$ identity matrix.\n\nFor any interval $K\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ containing at least two points, a map from $K$ is $C^1$ if it is continuous on $K$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and has at every included finite endpoint the corresponding one-sided derivative, with the derivative continuous there. A pathline is a $C^1$ map $x:\\mathcal J\\to\\mathbb R^3$, where $\\mathcal J\\subseteq I$ is an interval containing at least two points, such that $(t,x(t))\\in\\Omega$ and $x'(t)=u(t,x(t))$ for every $t\\in\\mathcal J$; derivatives at included finite endpoints are one-sided. Each curve $t\\mapsto\\chi(t,a)$ on $I$ is a pathline. For a fixed $t_0\\in I$, a streamline at frozen time $t_0$ is a $C^1$ map $X:\\mathcal S\\to\\chi_{t_0}(U)$, where $\\mathcal S\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ is an interval containing at least two points, satisfying $X'(s)=u(t_0,X(s))$ for every $s\\in\\mathcal S$; derivatives at included finite endpoints are one-sided. No equality between pathlines and frozen-time streamlines is part of this definition. These are mathematical kinematic definitions; no units or physical balance postulates are imposed.",

          "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open region, let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\\overline B$, and let $\\chi\\in C^2(I\\times U,\\mathbb R^3)$ be a family of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms $\\chi_t:U\\to\\chi_t(U)$ with $J(t,a):=\\det D_a\\chi(t,a)>0$. Here $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous; a diffeomorphism is a bijection with an inverse of the stated regularity. Write $A(t,x)=\\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, $u(t,x)=\\partial_t\\chi(t,A(t,x))$, $F=D_a\\chi$, $L=D_xu$, and $\\theta=\\operatorname{tr}L=\\sum_{i=1}^3\\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Here $D_a\\chi$ and $D_xu$ are matrices of coordinate partial derivatives. The joint inverse $A$ has domain $\\Omega=\\{(t,x):t\\in I,\\ x\\in\\chi_t(U)\\}$.\n\nA compact Jordan set $K\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ means a compact set whose boundary, for every $\\varepsilon>0$, is coverable by finitely many axis-parallel boxes with total volume less than $\\varepsilon$, where a box's volume is the product of its side lengths. Integrals over such sets are Riemann integrals, defined by extending the integrand by zero to a containing rectangle. Let $K\\subset U$ be any compact Jordan set and let $q,\\rho\\in C^1(\\Omega,\\mathbb R)$. Then $A$ is jointly $C^2$, and for every $a\\in U$ and $t\\in I$,\n\n$$\\partial_tF(t,a)=L(t,\\chi(t,a))F(t,a),\\qquad \\partial_tJ(t,a)=J(t,a)\\theta(t,\\chi(t,a)),\\qquad J(t,a)=J(0,a)\\exp\\!\\left(\\int_0^t\\theta(s,\\chi(s,a))\\,ds\\right).$$\n\nFor every $t\\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy\n\n$$\\int_{\\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\\,dx=\\int_Kq(t,\\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\\,da,$$\n\n$$\\frac{d}{dt}\\int_{\\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\\,dx=\\int_{\\chi_t(K)}\\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\\theta(t,x)\\bigr)\\,dx=\\int_{\\chi_t(K)}\\bigl(\\partial_tq+\\nabla_x\\!\\cdot(qu)\\bigr)\\,dx,$$\n\nwhere $D_tq=\\partial_tq+u\\cdot\\nabla_xq$ and $\\nabla_x\\!\\cdot(qu)=\\sum_{i=1}^3\\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\\int_{\\chi_t(K)}\\rho(t,x)\\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\\rho+\\rho\\theta=0$, equivalently $\\partial_t\\rho+\\nabla_x\\!\\cdot(\\rho u)=0$, holds on $\\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\\subset U$, and if and only if $\\rho(t,\\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\\rho(0,\\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\\in U$ and $t\\in I$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.",

Write $H(t,a):=(t,\\chi(t,a))$ and $\\Omega:=\\{(t,x):t\\in I,\\ x\\in\\chi_t(U)\\}$. The map $H$ is injective and its derivative is block triangular with determinant $J>0$, so the inverse function theorem gives local $C^1$ inverses; injectivity makes them agree on overlaps. Hence $\\Omega$ is open and the joint inverse $A(t,x):=\\chi_t^{-1}(x)$ is $C^1$. Define $u(t,x):=\\partial_t\\chi(t,A(t,x))$, which is $C^1$. For any $C^1$ vector field $f$ on $\\Omega$, let $D_xf$ be its matrix of spatial coordinate partial derivatives and define $D_tf:=\\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$.           "physical_scope": "Smooth nonrelativistic continuum kinematics on Newtonian spacetime, with explicit Cartesian inertial charts, rigid observers, material motions, field types, primitive/derived roles, and SI dimensions. No relativistic causal structure or empirical fluid applicability is asserted.",
          "inventory_expansion_required": false,
          "statement": "Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\\times E$, where $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\\to\\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\\mathrm{SO}(3)=\\{Q\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\\det Q=1\\}$. Inertial charts are related by\n\n$$t^*=t+t_0,\\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$\n\nwhere $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\\in\\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\\in C^2(I,\\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\\in C^2(I,\\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\\in C^2(I,\\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time.           "kind": "definition",
          "title": "Formal parameterized fluid systems and observables",
          "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\\rho:I\\times\\Omega\\to(0,\\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\\nabla f=(\\partial_{x_1}f,\\partial_{x_2}f,\\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\\operatorname{div}u=\\sum_{j=1}^3\\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\\operatorname{curl}u=(\\partial_{x_2}u_3-\\partial_{x_3}u_2,\\partial_{x_3}u_1-\\partial_{x_1}u_3,\\partial_{x_1}u_2-\\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\\Delta f=\\sum_{j=1}^3\\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\\in\\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\\cdot\\nabla)u=\\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\\partial_{x_j}u$.\n\nFor constants $\\rho_0>0$ and $\\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\\nu=\\mu/\\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is\n\n$$\\partial_tu+(u\\cdot\\nabla)u+\\rho_0^{-1}\\nabla p-\\nu\\Delta u=0,\\qquad \\operatorname{div}u=0.$$\n\nLet $I_3$ denote the $3\\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\\sigma=-pI_3+\\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\\rho_0^{-1}\\nabla p-\\nu\\Delta u=0$ together with $\\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.\n\nFor a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\\infty)\\to\\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\\rho$ is\n\n$$\\partial_t\\rho+\\operatorname{div}(\\rho u)=0,\\qquad \\partial_tu+(u\\cdot\\nabla)u=-\\rho^{-1}\\nabla(P(\\rho))-\\nabla V.$$\n\nAt a constant background density $\\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\\Omega\\in\\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\\partial_tu+2\\Omega\\times u=-\\nabla q$ and $\\operatorname{div}u=0$.\n\nThe vorticity field is $\\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\\sigma^{[t]}:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}$, $\\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\\sigma(t,x)$. If $\\gamma:[a,b]\\to\\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\\gamma(a)=\\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\\oint_\\gamma u^{[t]}\\cdot d\\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\\int_S u^{[t]}\\cdot n_S\\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\\in S$ is $\\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\\int_S\\sigma^{[t]}n_S\\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\\in I$ and $x\\in\\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\\to\\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\\times[0,1]\\to\\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\\partial_tX(t,\\theta)=u(t,X(t,\\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\\{x\\in\\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\\}\\subseteq\\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ or $f:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\\to f_\\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\\to\\infty$ means $\\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\\infty|\\to0$ in the scalar case and $\\sup_{|e|=1}\\|f(re)-f_\\infty\\|_2\\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\\to\\infty$.\n\nFor one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\\mathrm m$, $[t]=\\mathrm s$, $[u]=\\mathrm{m\\,s^{-1}}$, $[\\rho]=\\mathrm{kg\\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\\mu]=\\mathrm{Pa\\,s}$, $[\\nu]=\\mathrm{m^2\\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\\mathrm{m^2\\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\\Omega]=\\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\\operatorname{curl}u]=\\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\\mathrm{m^2\\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\\mathrm{m^3\\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\\rho_0,\\mu,P,V,\\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\\nu=\\mu/\\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.",

          "title": "Exact Reynolds and Mach nondimensionalization",
          "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ and $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $\\rho_0,\\mu,U,L,c>0$, and set $\\nu=\\mu/\\rho_0$, $\\operatorname{Re}=UL/\\nu$, and $\\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$. Define $T=Ut/L$, $X=x/L$, $I^*=\\{Ut/L:t\\in I\\}$, and $\\Omega^*=\\{x/L:x\\in\\Omega\\}$. For the incompressible branch, let $u:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let $p:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Write $u^*:I^*\\times\\Omega^*\\to\\mathbb R^3$ and $p^*:I^*\\times\\Omega^*\\to\\mathbb R$ for the corresponding fields with the same stated regularity. Set $u(t,x)=Uu^*(T,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\\mathrm{ref}}+\\rho_0U^2p^*(T,X)$, where $p_{\\mathrm{ref}}$ is constant. Then the original system is equivalent under this invertible change of variables to\n\n$$\\partial_Tu^*+(u^*\\cdot\\nabla_X)u^*=-\\nabla_Xp^*+\\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\\Delta_Xu^*,\\qquad \\operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$\n\nFor the barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\\infty)\\to\\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives with $P'(\\rho_0)=c^2>0$. Let $u:I\\times\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, let $\\rho:I\\times\\Omega\\to(0,\\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial partial derivatives, and let any potential $V$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. Write $u^*:I^*\\times\\Omega^*\\to\\mathbb R^3$, $\\rho^*:I^*\\times\\Omega^*\\to(0,\\infty)$, and $p^*:I^*\\times\\Omega^*\\to\\mathbb R$ for the rescaled fields with the corresponding stated regularity. Set $\\rho=\\rho_0\\rho^*$ and $P(\\rho)=P(\\rho_0)+\\rho_0c^2p^*$; if a potential is present, set $V=U^2V^*$ with $V^*:\\Omega^*\\to\\mathbb R$. Then the exact transformed equations are\n\n$$\\partial_T\\rho^*+\\operatorname{div}_X(\\rho^*u^*)=0,\\qquad \\partial_Tu^*+(u^*\\cdot\\nabla_X)u^*=-\\operatorname{Ma}^{-2}(\\rho^*)^{-1}\\nabla_Xp^*-\\nabla_XV^*.$$\n\nThese are coefficient identities under positive changes of scale.           "title": "Finite-depth gravity-wave dispersion with quantitative limits",
          "statement": "Let $h,g,k>0$, let $a\\in\\mathbb R$, and set $s=kh$ and $\\omega=\\sqrt{gk\\tanh(s)}$, using the positive square root. Here $h$ is depth, $g$ a constant acceleration parameter, and $k$ a positive horizontal wave number; $s$ is dimensionless and $a$ is a real elevation amplitude. The strict positivity of $\\tanh(s)$ for $s>0$ makes $\\omega$ well-defined and positive. Let $x,y\\in\\mathbb R$ be horizontal Cartesian coordinates and $z\\in(-h,0)$ the vertical coordinate, positive upward with the flat mean surface at $z=0$ and bottom at $z=-h$; time $t\\in\\mathbb R$. Write $\\theta=kx-\\omega t$. A surface elevation is the scalar field $\\eta(t,x,y)$, and a velocity potential is a scalar field $\\phi(t,x,y,z)$. Define the finite-depth linear potential-wave problem by\n\n$$\\Delta\\phi=0\\quad(-h<z<0),\\qquad \\phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$\n\n$$\\eta_t(t,x,y)=\\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\\qquad \\phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$\n\nwhere $\\Delta=\\partial_x^2+\\partial_y^2+\\partial_z^2$. Let $S,C$ be the real sine and cosine functions defined on this page. Then\n\n$$\\eta(t,x,y)=aC(\\theta),\\qquad \\phi(t,x,y,z)=\\frac{ag}{\\omega}\\frac{\\cosh(k(z+h))}{\\cosh(kh)}S(\\theta)$$\n\nare fields that are $C^2$ in the spatial variables and $C^1$ in time, with the displayed derivatives extending to $z=-h$ and $z=0$, and they satisfy this system exactly. Define the shallow and deep comparison frequencies by $\\omega_{\\rm sh}=k\\sqrt{gh}$ and $\\omega_{\\rm deep}=\\sqrt{gk}$. They obey\n\n$$0\\le\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm sh}^2-\\omega^2}{\\omega_{\\rm sh}^2}\\le\\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\\qquad 0\\le1-\\frac{\\omega}{\\omega_{\\rm sh}}\\le\\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\\qquad 0\\le\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm deep}^2-\\omega^2}{\\omega_{\\rm deep}^2}\\le2e^{-2kh}.$$\n\nThese are exact statements about the displayed linear boundary problem and its dispersion relation. They assert no nonlinear free-surface solution or error bound.\n\nIn the optional SI interpretation, $[h]=\\mathrm m$, $[g]=\\mathrm{m\\,s^{-2}}$, $[k]=\\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[a]=[\\eta]=\\mathrm m$, $[\\omega]=\\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $[\\phi]=\\mathrm{m^2\\,s^{-1}}$.",

          "title": "Locally integrable conservative weak and initial forms",
          "statement": "Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\\mathbb R^n,\\mathcal L_n,\\lambda_n)$, where $\\mathcal L_n=\\mathcal L(\\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\\mathcal L_E:=\\{E\\cap B:B\\in\\mathcal L_n\\}$ and the measure $\\lambda_E(A):=\\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\\in\\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\\to\\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\\in\\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\\subseteq\\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\\lambda_E$-null set. Nonnegative integrals are suprema of nonnegative simple minorants; signed real integrals are the difference of the positive- and negative-part integrals when those parts are finite. Finite-dimensional integrals are taken componentwise.\n\nLet $T>0$, let $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\\ge1$ be an integer. Put $D:=\\Omega\\times[0,T)\\subseteq\\mathbb R^4$ in spatial-first coordinates $(x,t)$. Both $D$ and $\\Omega$ are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. Spatial integrals use $\\lambda_\\Omega$ from $\\lambda_3$, and space-time integrals use $\\lambda_D$ from $\\lambda_4$. For a finite coordinate array $v$, set $\\|v\\|_1:=\\sum_i|v_i|$, summing all entries for a matrix. A measurable field $f:E\\to\\mathbb R^k$ is locally integrable when $\\int_K\\|f\\|_1\\,d\\lambda_E<\\infty$ for every compact $K\\subseteq E$. For $E=D$ the compact sets are taken in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields on $D$ are identified up to $\\lambda_D$-almost-everywhere equality, and initial fields on $\\Omega$ up to $\\lambda_\\Omega$-almost-everywhere equality. The slice $\\Omega\\times\\{0\\}$ is contained in a Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplane in $\\mathbb R^4$; values of a space-time representative on that slice do not determine the separately prescribed initial field.\n\nIn the displayed weak identities, $\\int_0^T\\int_\\Omega f\\,dx\\,dt$ denotes the joint integral of the zero extension of $f$ from $D$ with respect to $\\lambda_4$. For each test, its compact support bounds the test and its first derivatives, so every component of the tested products is measurable and is bounded in absolute value by a fixed multiple of the norm of a locally integrable field on that compact set. Thus all tested products and their finite sums have finite signed integrals. Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R$ is the completed product of $\\lambda_3$ and $\\lambda_1$; completed-product Fubini therefore also gives the displayed iterated notation, with section integrals taken for almost every time and set to zero on a measurable exceptional null set. No integrability of every individual time slice is required. The integral is unchanged by the stated almost-everywhere identifications. The same conventions apply to the scalar inequality and to the initial integrals on $\\Omega$.\n\nLet $U: \\Omega\\times[0,T)\\to\\mathbb R^m$, $F: \\Omega\\times[0,T)\\to\\mathbb R^{m\\times3}$, and $S: \\Omega\\times[0,T)\\to\\mathbb R^m$ be such fields, and let $U_0:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^m$ be locally integrable. For each row $a$, define $(\\operatorname{div}_x F)_a=\\sum_{j=1}^3\\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$ in the distributional sense, and define $F:\\nabla_x\\phi=\\sum_{a=1}^m\\sum_{j=1}^3F_{aj}\\partial_{x_j}\\phi_a$. The equation $\\partial_tU+\\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ with distributional initial datum $U_0$ means that for every $\\phi\\in C_c^1(\\Omega\\times[0,T);\\mathbb R^m)$, continuously differentiable up to $t=0$ and supported away from $\\partial\\Omega$ and $t=T$,\n\n$$\\int_0^T\\!\\int_\\Omega\\bigl(U\\cdot\\partial_t\\phi+F:\\nabla_x\\phi+S\\cdot\\phi\\bigr)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega U_0(x)\\cdot\\phi(x,0)\\,dx=0.$$\n\nNo boundary condition on $\\partial\\Omega$ is encoded because the test fields are supported away from it. This initial identity specifies the initial datum distributionally; it does not assert $U(\\cdot,t)\\to U_0$ in $L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(\\Omega)$ or any other stronger trace topology. Such a trace must be assumed or proved separately. The fields are abstract mathematical variables; no physical unit system or balance postulate is imposed.\n\nFor locally integrable scalar fields $H,R:D\\to\\mathbb R$ and $H_0:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$, and a locally integrable flux $Q: \\Omega\\times[0,T)\\to\\mathbb R^3$, the inequality $\\partial_tH+\\operatorname{div}_x Q\\ge R$ with initial datum $H_0$ means that for every nonnegative $\\psi\\in C_c^1(\\Omega\\times[0,T))$ with the same support convention,\n\n$$\\int_0^T\\!\\int_\\Omega\\bigl(H\\,\\partial_t\\psi+Q\\cdot\\nabla_x\\psi+R\\psi\\bigr)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega H_0(x)\\psi(x,0)\\,dx\\le0.$$",

          "kind": "lemma",
          "title": "Linear traction from shrinking local contact balance",
          "statement": "Assume the axiom of countable choice: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\\in\\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a selector $f$ with $f(n)\\in X_n$. Let $I\\subset\\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, and let $U\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\\overline B\\subset U$. Let $\\chi\\in C^2(I\\times U;\\mathbb R^3)$ have slices $\\chi_t:U\\to\\chi_t(U)$ that are bijections with $C^2$ inverses and $\\det D_a\\chi(t,a)>0$ for all $a\\in U$. Write $\\Omega_t=\\chi_t(B)$ and $\\mathcal Q=\\{(s,y):s\\in I,\\ y\\in\\Omega_s\\}$, and for $(t,x)\\in\\mathcal Q$ define $A(t,x)=\\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, $u(t,x)=\\partial_t\\chi(t,A(t,x))$, and $D_tf=\\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$; define the material acceleration $a_m:=D_tu$. At a fixed $(t,x)\\in\\mathcal Q$, let $\\rho:\\mathcal Q\\to(0,\\infty)$ and $b:\\mathcal Q\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be continuously differentiable nearby. Let $\\tau:\\mathcal Q\\times S^2\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be a contact traction indexed by the point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\\in S^2$. In SI units, spatial and reference coordinates are measured in metres, $t$ in seconds, $\\rho$ in $\\mathrm{kg\\,m^{-3}}$, $b$ and $a_m$ in $\\mathrm{m\\,s^{-2}}$, and $\\tau$ in pascals, so both terms in the assumed resultant balance have units of newtons. Assume $\\tau$ depends on a contact surface only through $(t,y,n)$, is continuous in $(y,n)$, and is uniformly bounded near $(t,x)$ for $n\\in S^2$.\n\nFor every nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $P$ whose closure is a compact subset of $\\Omega_t$, meaning that its boundary is locally a $C^1$ graph and $P$ lies locally on one side, suppose the local force balance\n$$\\int_{\\partial P}\\tau(t,y,\\nu_P(y))\\,dS_y+\\int_P\\rho(t,y)\\bigl(b(t,y)-a_m(t,y)\\bigr)\\,dy=0$$\nholds, where $\\nu_P$ is the outward unit normal and $dS$ is Euclidean surface measure defined in regular charts by the Gram density $\\sqrt{\\det(DX^TDX)}$. Then there is a unique matrix $\\sigma(t,x)\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}$ such that $\\tau(t,x,n)=\\sigma(t,x)n$ for every $n\\in S^2$. This conclusion assumes ordinary surface traction with no surface couples or curvature-dependent singular forces.",

The pointwise strong equations below are hypotheses on already-existing fields; no existence claim or inference from the integral balances alone is made.\n\nLet $\\Omega\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected open $C^1$ domain, meaning that each boundary point has a neighborhood in which the boundary is a $C^1$ graph and $\\Omega$ lies on one side of that graph after a rigid coordinate change. Let $C_\\Omega>0$ have units of metres and satisfy $\\|v\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)}\\le C_\\Omega\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)}$ for every $v\\in C^1(\\overline\\Omega;\\mathbb R^3)$ with zero boundary trace. The second is the separately adopted restricted steady Stokes comparison system, with its convective term omitted only for $u_{\\rm S}$. Define $w=u_{\\rm NS}-u_{\\rm S}$, $\\pi=p_{\\rm NS}-p_{\\rm S}$, and $f=-\\rho_0(u_{\\rm NS}\\cdot\\nabla)u_{\\rm NS}$. Then\n\n$$\\|\\nabla w\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)}\\le \\frac{C_\\Omega}{\\mu}\\|f\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)},\\qquad \\|w\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)}\\le \\frac{C_\\Omega^2}{\\mu}\\|f\\|_{L^2(\\Omega)}.$$\n\nFor a periodic channel $Q=\\mathbb T_{L_x}\\times(0,h)\\times\\mathbb T_{L_z}$, with $L_x,L_z,h>0$ measured in metres and $\\mathbb T_L=\\mathbb R/(L\\mathbb Z)$, take periodic fields in the two torus coordinates and integrate over one fundamental cell using Lebesgue measure. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\\to\\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\\in\\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\\widehat q(k)=\\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\\cdot x}\\,d\\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\\in L^1$.           "statement": "Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\\in\\{1,2,3\\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\\mathbb R^d/(2\\pi\\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\\mu=(2\\pi)^{-d}dx$. For a map $z:[0,T]\\times Q_d\\to\\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\\in\\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\\alpha$, $\\partial_t^m\\partial_x^\\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\\ne0$.           "kind": "theorem",
          "title": "Rectangular no-slip Stokes velocity and distribution pressure",
          "statement": "Assume full AC. Let $d\\ge2$, $R>0$, and let $\\Omega=\\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)\\subset(-R,R)^d$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. For $\\alpha=(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_d)\\in\\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\\alpha|=\\sum_j\\alpha_j$ and $\\partial^\\alpha=\\partial_1^{\\alpha_1}\\cdots\\partial_d^{\\alpha_d}$. For each compact $K\\subset\\Omega$, let $\\mathcal D_K(\\Omega)=\\{\\phi\\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega;\\mathbb R):\\operatorname{supp}\\phi\\subseteq K\\}$ with seminorms $p_{K,m}(\\phi)=\\max_{|\\alpha|\\le m}\\sup_{x\\in K}|\\partial^\\alpha\\phi(x)|$, $m\\in\\mathbb N_0$. Give $\\mathcal D(\\Omega)=C_c^\\infty(\\Omega;\\mathbb R)=\\bigcup_{K\\text{ compact},\\ K\\subset\\Omega}\\mathcal D_K(\\Omega)$ the locally convex inductive-limit topology of these fixed-support test spaces. Give vector test fields the componentwise topology. A scalar or vector distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on the corresponding test space; write its bilinear real pairing as $\\langle T,\\phi\\rangle$ or $\\langle T,\\psi\\rangle$. For scalar distributions define $\\langle\\partial_jT,\\phi\\rangle=-\\langle T,\\partial_j\\phi\\rangle$. For a smooth vector field $\\psi=(\\psi_1,\\ldots,\\psi_d)$, set $\\operatorname{div}\\psi=\\sum_j\\partial_j\\psi_j$ and $\\langle\\nabla p,\\psi\\rangle=-\\langle p,\\operatorname{div}\\psi\\rangle$. An $L^2$ vector field $f$ acts by $\\langle f,\\psi\\rangle=\\int_\\Omega f\\cdot\\psi\\,dx$, and for $u\\in H_0^1$ define $\\langle\\Delta u,\\psi\\rangle=-\\int_\\Omega\\nabla u:\\nabla\\psi\\,dx$.           "statement": "Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\\in\\{1,2,3\\}$, $\\ell>0$, and $\\nu\\ge0$, and write $Q_\\ell=\\mathbb R^d/(\\ell\\mathbb Z)^d$. For a period cell, define $\\|f\\|_{L^2_{\\rm vol}(Q_\\ell)}=(\\int_{[0,\\ell]^d}|f(x)|^2dx)^{1/2}$.\n\nFirst, for $T>0$ and either $\\Omega=\\mathbb R^d$ or $\\Omega=Q_\\ell$, let $u\\in C^\\infty([0,T]\\times\\Omega;\\mathbb R^d)$ and $\\pi\\in C^\\infty([0,T]\\times\\Omega;\\mathbb R)$ be a velocity-pressure pair solving the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes system\n$$u_t+(u\\cdot\\nabla)u=-\\nabla\\pi+\\nu\\Delta u,\\qquad \\operatorname{div}u=0,$$\nthen for any $\\lambda>0$,\n$$u_\\lambda(t,x)=\\lambda u(\\lambda^2t,\\lambda x),\\qquad \\pi_\\lambda(t,x)=\\lambda^2\\pi(\\lambda^2t,\\lambda x)$$\nsolves the same system with the same viscosity on $\\mathbb R^d$ or on the torus of period $\\ell/\\lambda$, respectively, for $0\\le t\\le T/\\lambda^2$. On the torus, use the Fourier Leray multiplier $P_0=I$, $P_\\xi=I-\\xi\\xi^{\\mathsf T}/|\\xi|^2$ for $\\xi\\ne0$; the projected equation is preserved as well because $P_{\\lambda\\xi}=P_\\xi$. For a cell-volume $L^2$ norm, $\\|u_\\lambda(0)\\|_{L^2_{\\rm vol}(Q_{\\ell/\\lambda})}=\\lambda^{1-d/2}\\|u(0)\\|_{L^2_{\\rm vol}(Q_\\ell)}$.\n\nSecond, for any $\\alpha,\\beta>0$, if $T>0$, $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^d$ is open, $u\\in C^\\infty([0,T]\\times\\Omega;\\mathbb R^d)$, and $\\pi\\in C^\\infty([0,T]\\times\\Omega;\\mathbb R)$ solve the unforced incompressible Euler system $u_t+(u\\cdot\\nabla)u=-\\nabla\\pi$, $\\operatorname{div}u=0$, then on the scaled domain $\\beta^{-1}\\Omega$,\n$$u_{\\alpha,\\beta}(t,x)=\\alpha u(\\alpha\\beta t,\\beta x),\\qquad \\pi_{\\alpha,\\beta}(t,x)=\\alpha^2\\pi(\\alpha\\beta t,\\beta x)$$\nsolves the same equation on the correspondingly scaled domain and time interval $0\\le t\\le T/(\\alpha\\beta)$. These transformations are equation symmetries; on a torus they transform its period.\n\nFinally, let $U,L,\\rho_*,\\eta>0$ be physical scales in SI units, where $U$ is in m/s, $L$ in m, $\\rho_*$ is a constant positive reference density in kg/m$^3$, and dynamic viscosity $\\eta$ is in Pa$\\cdot$s. Set kinematic viscosity $\\nu=\\eta/\\rho_*$, in m$^2$/s. Let $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^d$ be an open dimensionless spatial region and $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ an open time interval; set $\\Omega_{\\rm phys}=L\\Omega$ and $I_{\\rm phys}=(L/U)I$. Take $u,v\\in C^\\infty(\\Omega\\times I;\\mathbb R^d)$ and $\\pi,\\delta\\rho'\\in C^\\infty(\\Omega\\times I;\\mathbb R)$; the scaled fields $u,v,\\pi,\\delta\\rho'$ are dimensionless. Define physical velocity maps $u_{\\rm phys},v_{\\rm phys}\\in C^\\infty(\\Omega_{\\rm phys}\\times I_{\\rm phys};\\mathbb R^d)$, physical-pressure maps $p_{\\rm phys},\\pi_{\\rm phys}\\in C^\\infty(\\Omega_{\\rm phys}\\times I_{\\rm phys};\\mathbb R)$, and density-perturbation map $\\delta\\rho\\in C^\\infty(\\Omega_{\\rm phys}\\times I_{\\rm phys};\\mathbb R)$ by\n$$u_{\\rm phys}(X,t_{\\rm phys})=Uu(X/L,Ut_{\\rm phys}/L),\\quad p_{\\rm phys}(X,t_{\\rm phys})=\\rho_*U^2\\pi(X/L,Ut_{\\rm phys}/L),$$\n$$v_{\\rm phys}(X,t_{\\rm phys})=Uv(X/L,Ut_{\\rm phys}/L),\\quad \\delta\\rho(X,t_{\\rm phys})=\\rho_*\\delta\\rho'(X/L,Ut_{\\rm phys}/L).$$\nAdopt the constant-reference-density kinematic-pressure convention $\\pi_{\\rm phys}:=p_{\\rm phys}/\\rho_*$; thus $\\pi_{\\rm phys}=U^2\\pi$ has units m$^2$/s$^2$, while $p_{\\rm phys}$ has units Pa. If $u_{\\rm phys},\\pi_{\\rm phys}$ satisfy the constant-density incompressible system\n$$\\partial_{t_{\\rm phys}}u_{\\rm phys}+(u_{\\rm phys}\\cdot\\nabla_X)u_{\\rm phys}=-\\nabla_X\\pi_{\\rm phys}+\\nu\\Delta_Xu_{\\rm phys},\\qquad \\operatorname{div}_Xu_{\\rm phys}=0,$$\nthen the stated substitution gives the dimensionless system\n$$\\partial_tu+(u\\cdot\\nabla_x)u=-\\nabla_x\\pi+Re^{-1}\\Delta_xu,\\qquad \\operatorname{div}_xu=0,$$\nwhere $Re=UL/\\nu=\\rho_*UL/\\eta$. Let $p_{\\rm eos}:(0,\\infty)\\to\\mathbb R$ be a differentiable equation-of-state pressure map, measured in Pa, at $\\rho_*$, with $p_{\\rm eos}'(\\rho_*)>0$ in m$^2$/s$^2$, and set the sound speed $c_*=\\sqrt{p_{\\rm eos}'(\\rho_*)}$ in m/s. For the linear acoustic tangent system, let the physical fields $\\delta\\rho:\\Omega_{\\rm phys}\\times I_{\\rm phys}\\to\\mathbb R$ and $v_{\\rm phys}:\\Omega_{\\rm phys}\\times I_{\\rm phys}\\to\\mathbb R^d$ satisfy\n$$\\partial_{t_{\\rm phys}}\\delta\\rho+\\rho_*\\operatorname{div}_Xv_{\\rm phys}=0,\\qquad \\partial_{t_{\\rm phys}}v_{\\rm phys}+(c_*^2/\\rho_*)\\nabla_X\\delta\\rho=0.$$\nHere $\\delta\\rho$ has units kg/m$^3$. The scales $X=Lx$, $t_{\\rm phys}=(L/U)t$, $\\delta\\rho=\\rho_*\\delta\\rho'$, and $v_{\\rm phys}=Uv$ give the momentum coefficient $Ma^{-2}$, where $Ma=U/c_*$. Both $Re$ and $Ma$ are dimensionless.           "inventory_expansion_required": false,
          "statement": "Let $d\\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed\nlength unit. Let\n$\\mathbb T_L^d=(\\mathbb R/L\\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure\n$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\\in\\mathbb Z^d$ put\n$\\kappa_k=2\\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\\exp(i\\kappa_k\\cdot x)$. For a complex\nscalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let\n$\\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\\kappa_k\\cdot x}\\,dx$;\nreal fields are the classes satisfying\n$\\widehat f(-k)=\\overline{\\widehat f(k)}$. For $s\\ge0$, let\n$$H^s(\\mathbb T_L^d)=\\left\\{f\\in L^2:\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\\kappa_k|^2)^s|\\widehat f(k)|^2<\\infty\\right\\},$$\nwith norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.\nUnder Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.\nThe real solenoidal spaces are\n$$H=\\{u\\in L^2(\\mathbb T_L^d;\\mathbb R^d): k\\cdot\\widehat u(k)=0\\text{ for every }k\\ne0\\},\\qquad V=H\\cap H^1(\\mathbb T_L^d;\\mathbb R^d).$$\nThe zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied\nFourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from\n$L^2$ onto $\\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the\nequivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this\ndefinition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal\nsolenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier\n$P_0=I$ and\n$P_k=I-\\kappa_k\\kappa_k^{\\mathsf T}/|\\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\\ne0$. For integer\n$N\\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\\infty\\le N$. A weak\nderivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\\kappa_{k,j}\\widehat f(k)$.\nFor $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier\ncoefficient sequences in the norm squared\n$\\sum_k(1+L^2|\\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the\ncompletion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.",

          "statement": "Let $\\mathbb K\\in\\{\\mathbb R,\\mathbb C\\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over\n$\\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\\mathbb K$, and let\n$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\\to H$\nsuch that $t\\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\\in H$;\nmembership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence\nclass. A map $u:(0,T)\\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere\npointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\\le p<\\infty$,\n$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly\nmeasurable maps with $\\int_0^T\\|u(t)\\|_X^pdt<\\infty$; $L^\\infty(0,T;X)$\nconsists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,\n$L^p_{\\rm loc}(0,\\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval\n$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$\nand to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$\nis separable.\n\nIf two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree\nat every $t\\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most\none weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise\nvalues associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.",

          "statement": "Let $d\\ge2$, $L>0$, $\\nu>0$, $u_0\\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time\nconventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and\nWeak time continuity and energy spaces. All clauses\ninvolving $u(t)$ at a specified time, including the initial trace and energy\ninequalities, refer to this weakly continuous map.           "statement": "Fix a constant $\gamma>1$. The one-dimensional ideal-gas Euler state is
$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathcal G_\gamma\subset\mathbb R^3$, where
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\}.$$
For $U\in\mathcal G_\gamma$, define the pressure, velocity, sound speed, and
flux by
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right),\qquad u(U)=\frac m\rho,\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}},\qquad F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(U)(E+p(U))\right).$$
Thus $\mathcal G_\gamma$ is exactly the set with positive density and positive
pressure; every displayed map is defined on that open set.

For a periodic uniform mesh with $N\ge2$ cells, width $\Delta x>0$, and time
step $\Delta t\ge0$, index cells by $i\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and put
$\lambda=\Delta t/\Delta x$. Given cell states $U_i\in\mathcal G_\gamma$, a
shared-face flux is one vector $\widehat F_{i+1/2}\in\mathbb R^3$ assigned to
each face and used in both adjacent cell balances. When produced by a
two-state numerical flux $\widehat F(U_L,U_R)$, it is consistent if
$\widehat F(U,U)=F(U)$ for every $U\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. The associated
one-step update in conservative finite-volume form is
$$U_i^+=U_i-\lambda\left(\widehat F_{i+1/2}-\widehat F_{i-1/2}\right).$$
This shared-face form means that the same face vector appears with opposite
signs in the two neighboring cell updates. A step is admissible when every
output state $U_i^+$ belongs to $\mathcal G_\gamma$; this is a property to
prove under specific flux and time-step hypotheses, not part of the update
definition.

When the HLL middle branch is used at a face, its supplied speeds satisfy
$S_L<0<S_R$ and the flux is
$$\widehat F_{\rm HLL}(U_L,U_R)=\frac{S_RF(U_L)-S_LF(U_R)+S_LS_R(U_R-U_L)}{S_R-S_L}.$$
The speeds are supplied data; their appearance in this formula does not assert
that they enclose the waves of an exact nonlinear Riemann solution. The
ratio $\lambda$ is the time step divided by cell width and is not a physical
viscosity.

For a specified convex entropy pair, write $v$ for its entropy variable and
$F^{ec}$ for a consistent entropy-conservative two-point flux. If $D$ is a
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix, meaning $z^TDz\ge0$ for every vector
$z$, and $F^{ec}$ satisfies
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^T F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi(U_R)-\psi(U_L),$$
where $\psi$ is the corresponding entropy potential, the entropy-stable
dissipative flux is
$$F^{es}(U_L,U_R)=F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)-\frac12D(U_L,U_R)\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr).$$
Here $v=\nabla\eta$ for the chosen entropy $\eta$, and the entropy-conservative
flux satisfies the corresponding entropy-variable jump identity. This is a
separate flux condition; it includes no fully discrete time-step entropy
inequality. Conservation, admissibility, entropy stability, and convergence
therefore name different properties and require their own hypotheses.

The entropy-stable dissipative-flux definition specifies a consistent
entropy-conservative flux with positive-semidefinite entropy-variable
dissipation, and explicitly supplies no fully discrete time-step inequality.
Any semidiscrete entropy inequality for a selected semidiscrete evolution is a
separate result; a fully discrete bound also requires an argument for the
chosen time integrator. The ratio $\nu$ above is only the mesh time-step to
width ratio and is not physical viscosity.

For the convex-scaling limiter, assume additionally that $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
is closed, meaning it contains every limit in $\mathbb R^m$ of a convergent
sequence of its members; $K$ remains convex. The limiter applies to a finite nonempty set of node states
$V_j\in\mathbb R^m$ with positive weights $w_j$ summing to one and an already
admissible mean $\bar V=\sum_jw_jV_j\in K$. It returns the largest
$\theta\in[0,1]$ for which all scaled states
$V_j^\theta=\bar V+\theta(V_j-\bar V)$ belong to $K$. The feasible parameter
set is closed in $[0,1]$ and contains $0$, so this maximum exists. Direct summation gives
$$\sum_jw_jV_j^\theta=\sum_jw_j\bar V+\theta\left(\sum_jw_jV_j-\sum_jw_j\bar V\right)=\bar V+\theta(\bar V-\bar V)=\bar V.$$
Thus the construction preserves the supplied mean and constrains the chosen
nodes; it has no admissibility branch for a mean outside $K$ and gives no
pointwise-in-cell assertion between those nodes.

The conservative finite-volume weak-limit theorem is a separate scalar
one-dimensional result on $\mathbb R$. It assumes $T>0$, a continuous scalar
flux $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, initial data
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, a continuous
consistent numerical flux $F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$, initial cell averages,
$h_m,\tau_m\to0$, and the Axiom of Countable Choice
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ (for every family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets,
there is a function $f:\mathbb N\to\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}X_n$ with
$f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$). Strong local $L^1$ convergence of the reconstructed states and
local uniform bounds on every bounded space-time cylinder through $t=0$ are
also hypotheses. Under them the limit is a locally bounded scalar
distributional weak solution. In its proof, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only
in the local spatial-translation step of the face-flux convergence lemma; the
discrete summation and limit passage require no further choice. The theorem
assumes neither a CFL condition nor

          "statement": "Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an event-coordinate map with absolute-time coordinate and spatial maps $X_t(q)=b(q)+tw$, where $b:M\\to\\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres per second. Write $X=(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ for the spatial event coordinates of one selected such chart. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\\Omega\\times(0,T_f)$. For this one-dimensional weak branch, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and use the all-dimensional Euclidean Lebesgue convention of the conservative weak-form definition. Space-time fields use the restriction of $\\lambda_2$ to $\\Omega\\times[0,T_f)$ and initial data the restriction of $\\lambda_1$ to $\\Omega$, with the corresponding trace sigma-algebras, measurable-map and almost-everywhere conventions. Integrals use the signed Lebesgue integral and completed-product almost-everywhere section convention from that definition. The measurable fields are mass density $\\rho:\\Omega\\times(0,T_f)\\to(0,\\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\\Omega\\times(0,T_f)\\to\\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\\Omega\\times(0,T_f)\\to\\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.\n\nAdopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\\mathcal U=(0,\\infty)\\times\\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\\mathcal U\\to\\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the adopted specific-heat-at-constant-volume parameter and $R>0$ the adopted specific gas-constant parameter, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\\in\\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation\n$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\\left(\\frac{v_*}{v}\\right)^{\\gamma-1}\\exp\\left(\\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\\right),$$\nwith the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives\n$$T(v,s)=\\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\\qquad p(v,s)=(\\gamma-1)\\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$\nFor density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s):=p(1/\\rho,s)$ for $\\rho>0$ and $s\\in\\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\\in\\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by\n$$e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\\qquad T(t,x):=(\\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\\qquad p_{\\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$\nConsequently $T(t,x)=e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\\gamma-1)e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\\gamma-1)\\rho(t,x)e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\\rho^\\gamma$, so $\\left.\\partial_\\rho p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s)\\right|_s=\\gamma p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s)/\\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s):=\\sqrt{\\left.\\partial_\\rho p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s)\\right|_s}=\\sqrt{\\gamma p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s)/\\rho}$. Thus $\\gamma$ is dimensionless, sound speed has units of metres per second, and pressure has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.\n\nDefine momentum density $m(t,x):=\\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\\rho(t,x)(e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. The corresponding numerical state is $U(t,x):=(\\rho(t,x),m(t,x),E(t,x))\\in\\mathbb R^3$. For $\\gamma>1$, set\n$$\\mathcal G_\\gamma=\\left\\{(\\rho,m,E):\\rho>0,\\quad E-\\frac{m^2}{2\\rho}>0\\right\\},\\qquad p(U)=(\\gamma-1)\\left(E-\\frac{m^2}{2\\rho}\\right).$$\nSince $\\rho(t,x)>0$ and $e_{\\mathrm{int}}(t,x)>0$, $U(t,x)\\in\\mathcal G_\\gamma$. For this state, $E-m^2/(2\\rho)=\\rho e_{\\mathrm{int}}$ and $p(U(t,x))=p_{\\mathrm{th}}(t,x)$, so the numerical and thermodynamic pressure maps agree. With $u=m/\\rho$, its one-dimensional Euler flux and isentropic sound speed are\n$$F(U)=\\left(m,\\frac{m^2}{\\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\\right),\\qquad c(U)=\\sqrt{\\frac{\\gamma p(U)}{\\rho}}.$$\nThe components of $F$ are mass flux in kilograms per square metre second, momentum flux in pascals, and energy flux in watts per square metre. The speed $c$ is in metres per second.\n\nAdopt the inviscid one-dimensional branch with zero body acceleration, zero specific heat supply, zero conductive heat flux, and isotropic three-dimensional Cauchy stress $\\sigma=-p_{\\mathrm{th}}I_3$ in the tension-positive convention in which traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\\sigma n$; here $I_3$ is the $3\\times3$ identity matrix. Its restriction to the selected axis is the scalar normal stress $\\sigma_{\\mathrm{1D}}:=\\sigma_{11}=-p_{\\mathrm{th}}$ in pascals, so the one-dimensional momentum flux is $\\rho u^2-\\sigma_{\\mathrm{1D}}=\\rho u^2+p_{\\mathrm{th}}$. In the following weak identities, write $p:=p_{\\mathrm{th}}$. Assume the locally integrable conservative variables, fluxes, entropy density, and entropy flux satisfy the identities in the distributional sense. Let $\\rho_0,m_0,E_0,S_0\\in L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(\\Omega)$ be the initial mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, momentum density in kilograms per square metre second, total energy density in joules per cubic metre, and entropy density in joules per cubic metre kelvin, respectively. Require all displayed densities, fluxes, and products to be locally integrable up to $t=0$: their absolute values have finite integrals on every compact subset of $\\Omega\\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using the fields for $t>0$. This requirement assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Test functions $\\phi,\\psi,\\eta,\\zeta\\in C^1(\\Omega\\times[0,T_f))$ are compactly supported in space-time and vanish near $T_f$; $\\zeta$ is nonnegative, and tests may be nonzero at $t=0$. Then adopt\n$$\\int_0^{T_f}\\!\\!\\int_\\Omega\\left(\\rho\\,\\partial_t\\phi+\\rho u\\,\\partial_x\\phi\\right)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega\\rho_0\\phi(0,x)\\,dx=0,$$\n$$\\int_0^{T_f}\\!\\!\\int_\\Omega\\left(\\rho u\\,\\partial_t\\psi+(\\rho u^2+p)\\partial_x\\psi\\right)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega m_0\\psi(0,x)\\,dx=0,$$\n$$\\int_0^{T_f}\\!\\!\\int_\\Omega\\left(E\\,\\partial_t\\eta+u(E+p)\\partial_x\\eta\\right)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega E_0\\eta(0,x)\\,dx=0,$$\nand\n$$\\int_0^{T_f}\\!\\!\\int_\\Omega\\left(\\rho s\\,\\partial_t\\zeta+\\rho u s\\,\\partial_x\\zeta\\right)\\,dx\\,dt+\\int_\\Omega S_0\\zeta(0,x)\\,dx\\le0.$$\nThe last inequality is a separately adopted physical entropy inequality. It is not deduced from the conservative equations or from smooth-flow identities. This postulate specifies a physical model and its idealized local-equilibrium closure; it does not assert existence or uniqueness of a weak solution, prove that actual matter obeys the model, or identify a computed state with an experimental observation.",

Its thermodynamic pressure map, for $\\rho>0$ and $s\\in\\mathbb R$, is\n$$p_{\\mathrm{th}}(\\rho,s):=R T_*v_*^{\\gamma-1}\\rho^\\gamma\\exp\\left(\\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\\right).$$\nIts admissible state set is\n$$\\mathcal G_\\gamma=\\left\\{(\\rho,m,E)\\in\\mathbb R^3:\\rho>0,\\quad E-\\frac{m^2}{2\\rho}>0\\right\\}.$$\nFor every $U=(\\rho,m,E)\\in\\mathcal G_\\gamma$, define velocity, specific internal energy, specific volume, and specific entropy by\n$$u(U):=\\frac m\\rho,\\qquad e_{\\mathrm{int}}(U):=\\frac E\\rho-\\frac{u(U)^2}{2},\\qquad v(U):=\\frac1\\rho,\\qquad s_{\\mathrm{th}}(U):=s_*+c_v\\log\\left(\\frac{e_{\\mathrm{int}}(U)}{c_vT_*}\\left(\\frac{v(U)}{v_*}\\right)^{\\gamma-1}\\right).$$\nHere $u(U)$ is velocity in metres per second, $e_{\\mathrm{int}}(U)>0$ is specific internal energy in joules per kilogram, and $v(U)$ is specific volume in cubic metres per kilogram. Define the numerical pressure and sound speed by\n$$p(U):=(\\gamma-1)\\left(E-\\frac{m^2}{2\\rho}\\right),\\qquad c(U):=\\sqrt{\\frac{\\gamma p(U)}\\rho}.$$\nHere $p(U)$ is pressure in pascals and $c(U)$ is speed in metres per second.           "statement": "Let $(D,\\mathcal D,\\lambda)$, $d$, and $H$ be as in the Definition, with $\\lambda(D)>0$. Let $e_1$ be the first standard basis vector in $\\mathbb R^d$ and set $\\psi:=e_1/\\lambda(D)$. For each $x\\in\\mathbb R$, the spatially uniform field $V_x(y):=x e_1$ belongs to $H$ and has sensor reading $S_\\psi(V_x)=x$.\n\nAssume AC. Let $(X_n)_{n\\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, jointly Gaussian time-homogeneous Markov chain on $\\mathbb R$ with invariant probability $\\nu=\\mathcal L(X_0)$ and recursion\n$$X_{n+1}=\\rho X_n+\\epsilon_{n+1},\\qquad |\\rho|<1,\\quad \\eta>0.$$\nAssume $(\\epsilon_{n})_{n\\ge1}$ is an independent sequence with common law $N(0,\\eta^2)$, independent of $X_0$; then the transition kernel is $P(x,\\cdot)=N(\\rho x,\\eta^2)$. Here $N(m,v)$, for $v>0$, is the normal law with density $(2\\pi v)^{-1/2}\\exp(-(x-m)^2/(2v))$. “Jointly Gaussian” means every finite real linear combination of chain coordinates is normally distributed; “strictly stationary” means every finite-dimensional law is unchanged by nonnegative integer time shifts. The associated velocity-field sensor output is $Y_n:=S_\\psi(V_{X_n})=X_n$. If $X_n$ has velocity units $\\mathrm{m\\,s^{-1}}$, then $\\epsilon_n$ has the same units, $\\rho$ is dimensionless, and the long-run variance has units $\\mathrm{m^2\\,s^{-2}}$. This is a mathematical model example, not a reported fluid measurement.\n\nFor $k\\ge0$, its covariance is\n$$\\gamma_k:=\\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)=\\frac{\\eta^2\\rho^k}{1-\\rho^2}.$$\nThe covariance series is absolutely summable, and the centered sensor sum satisfies\n$$\\frac1{\\sqrt n}\\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}Y_j\\Rightarrow N\\!\\left(0,\\frac{\\eta^2}{(1-\\rho)^2}\\right).$$\nConsequently its covariance long-run variance is $\\sigma_{\\mathrm{LR}}^2=\\eta^2/(1-\\rho)^2$.",

          "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice required by the normalized periodic torus convention.           "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and let $D\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open $C^2$ domain. Here a $C^2$ domain is a nonempty connected open set whose boundary near each of its points, after a rigid Cartesian change of coordinates, is the graph $s_3=b(s_1,s_2)$ of a $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\\mathbb R^2$, with the domain locally on one side of that graph. Use the Cartesian gradient, divergence, row-component Jacobian, and componentwise Laplacian on $D$. For constants $\\rho_0,\\nu>0$, a body acceleration $f\\in C(I\\times D;\\mathbb R^3)$, a velocity $w\\in C^1(I;C^2(D;\\mathbb R^3))$, and a scalar pressure $q\\in C(I;C^1(D))$, define the full momentum residual\n\n$$\\mathcal R(w,q):=\\partial_t w+(w\\cdot\\nabla)w+\\rho_0^{-1}\\nabla q-\\nu\\Delta w-f.$$\n\nThe forced constant-density incompressible model is $\\mathcal R(u,p)=0$ with $\\operatorname{div}u=0$. For boundary statements, $C^k(\\overline D)$ means restrictions of $C^k$ functions on an open neighborhood of $\\overline D$, with all derivatives through order $k$ restricted continuously to the closure. A classical boundary trace is the restriction of this continuous extension to $\\partial D$; it is independent of the extension. A common-wall comparison requires $u,v\\in C^1(I;C^2(\\overline D;\\mathbb R^3))$ in this convention, with $\\operatorname{div}u=\\operatorname{div}v=0$, and their classical traces agree with the same prescribed boundary velocity $\\gamma(t,\\cdot)$. The interior residual above remains defined for the stated interior regularity even when no wall trace is supplied. For a divergence-free comparison field $w\\in C^1(I;C^2(\\overline D;\\mathbb R^3))$ in this same boundary regularity class with a different trace, a divergence-free wall lift is a field $\\ell\\in C^1(I;C^2(\\overline D;\\mathbb R^3))$ in the same extension convention with $\\operatorname{div}\\ell=0$ and $\\ell|_{\\partial D}=w|_{\\partial D}-\\gamma$; whenever such a lift is supplied, the corrected field is $v=w-\\ell$ and its residual is $\\mathcal R(v,q)$. This definition asserts no lift exists for arbitrary boundary data.\n\nFor a flat periodic channel $D_{\\rm ch}=\\mathbb T_{L_x}\\times(0,h)\\times\\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\\mathbb T_L=\\mathbb R/(L\\mathbb Z)$ and $L_x,L_z,h>0$, a specific tangential lift for lower and upper wall defects $a(t)e_x$ and $b(t)e_x$ is\n\n$$\\ell(t,x,y,z)=\\bigl(a(t)(1-y/h)+b(t)y/h,\\,0,\\,0\\bigr).$$\n\nHere $e_x=(1,0,0)$, $a,b\\in C^1(I,\\mathbb R)$, and the channel is periodic in $x,z$ with physical walls $y=0,h$. This lift is defined only for the stated tangential wall-defect data.\n\nFor the capillary-gravity model, let $h,\\rho,g,L_x,L_y>0$, $\\sigma\\ge0$, use horizontal coordinates $(x,y)\\in\\mathbb T_{L_x}\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}$ and vertical coordinate $z\\in(-h,0)$, positive upward, with the flat mean surface at $z=0$. Let $\\eta\\in C^1(I;C^2(\\mathbb T_{L_x}\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}))$ be surface elevation and $\\phi\\in C^1(I;C^2(\\mathbb T_{L_x}\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}\\times[-h,0]))$ a real scalar velocity potential: the represented velocity is $u:=\\nabla\\phi=(\\phi_x,\\phi_y,\\phi_z)$, with no added uniform component.           "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\\in\\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $c$ with $c(n)\\in X_n$. For real vector fields $F,G\\in L^2(D;\\mathbb R^3)$, use the inner product $\\langle F,G\\rangle=\\int_D F(x)\\cdot G(x)\\,dx$ and its norm $\\|F\\|_{L^2(D)}=(\\int_D|F(x)|^2\\,dx)^{1/2}$. Set $A(t)=\\int_0^tL(s)\\,ds$.           "title": "Capillary-gravity dispersion and conserved linear surface energy",
          "statement": "Let $h,g,\\rho,k,L_y>0$, $\\sigma\\ge0$, and $a\\in\\mathbb R$. Set $\\lambda=2\\pi/k$ and $\\mathbb T_L=\\mathbb R/(L\\mathbb Z)$; use horizontal coordinates $(x,y)\\in\\mathbb T_\\lambda\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}$ and vertical coordinate $z\\in[-h,0]$, positive upward, with the mean surface at $z=0$. Define\n\n$$\\omega_\\sigma=\\sqrt{\\left(gk+\\frac{\\sigma}{\\rho}k^3\\right)\\tanh(kh)},\\qquad G(z)=\\frac{\\cosh(k(z+h))}{\\cosh(kh)},\\qquad \\theta_\\sigma=k\\widetilde x-\\omega_\\sigma t.$$\n\nOnly $S(\\theta_\\sigma)$ and $C(\\theta_\\sigma)$ are used: changing $\\widetilde x$ by $n\\lambda$, $n\\in\\mathbb Z$, changes the real phase by $2\\pi n$ and leaves these values unchanged. Thus the formulas below define fields on the torus rather than a globally real-valued phase there. The fields\n\n$$\\eta_\\sigma(t,x,y)=aC(\\theta_\\sigma),\\qquad \\phi_\\sigma(t,x,y,z)=\\frac{a\\omega_\\sigma}{k\\tanh(kh)}G(z)S(\\theta_\\sigma)$$\n\nare smooth, independent of $y$, periodic with horizontal periods $\\lambda,L_y$, and solve exactly the linear capillary-gravity potential equations\n\n$$\\Delta\\phi=0\\quad(-h<z<0),\\qquad \\phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$\n\n$$\\eta_t(t,x,y)=\\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\\qquad \\phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\\eta(t,x,y)-\\frac{\\sigma}{\\rho}\\Delta_H\\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$\n\nwhere $\\Delta=\\partial_x^2+\\partial_y^2+\\partial_z^2$ and $\\Delta_H=\\partial_x^2+\\partial_y^2$. Here $h$ is depth, $g$ gravitational acceleration, $\\rho$ constant density, $\\sigma$ surface tension, and $\\Delta_H$ is the horizontal Laplacian. In particular, the positive frequency obeys\n\n$$\\omega_\\sigma^2=\\left(gk+\\frac{\\sigma}{\\rho}k^3\\right)\\tanh(kh).$$\n\nAt $\\sigma=0$ this mode is exactly the finite-depth gravity-wave mode. For any $T>0$, let $\\eta\\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\\mathbb T_\\lambda\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}))$ and $\\phi\\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\\mathbb T_\\lambda\\times\\mathbb T_{L_y}\\times[-h,0]))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of the closed slab and satisfy the same equations. Define the energy in one horizontal cell by\n\n$$E(t)=\\frac{\\rho}{2}\\int_0^{L_y}\\int_0^\\lambda\\int_{-h}^0 (|\\phi_x|^2+|\\phi_y|^2+|\\phi_z|^2)\\,dz\\,dx\\,dy+\\frac{\\rho g}{2}\\int_0^{L_y}\\int_0^\\lambda\\eta^2\\,dx\\,dy+\\frac{\\sigma}{2}\\int_0^{L_y}\\int_0^\\lambda (|\\eta_x|^2+|\\eta_y|^2)\\,dx\\,dy.$$\n\nThen $E(t)$ is nonnegative and constant on $[0,T]$.           "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, with absolute time $t\\in I$ in seconds, and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean vector space, and no origin is distinguished. The adopted Newtonian spacetime is the product $I\\times E$. Define $\\mathrm{SO}(3):=\\{Q\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}:Q^{\\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\\ \\det Q=1\\}$. A classical Cartesian inertial chart on $I\\times E$ is the event-coordinate map $(t,X)\\mapsto(t,\\mathbf r_t(X))$, where there are a fixed $t_{\\rm ref}\\in I$, an orientation-preserving affine isometry $\\mathbf r_{t_{\\rm ref}}:E\\to\\mathbb R^3$ whose linear part lies in $\\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and a constant $w\\in\\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second such that $\\mathbf r_t(X)=\\mathbf r_{t_{\\rm ref}}(X)+w(t-t_{\\rm ref})$ for every $t\\in I$ and $X\\in E$. Thus each fixed-time spatial coordinate map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, and its coordinates are measured in metres. Inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\\mathbf r^*=Q\\mathbf r+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\\in\\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres per second, and $a\\in\\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres. Thus “frame” means this adapted event-coordinate map on Newtonian spacetime, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Write the selected chart coordinates as $(x_1,x_2,z)$, with horizontal coordinate $x=(x_1,x_2)$ and upward vertical coordinate $z$, all in metres, and let $e_z$ be the upward unit vector.\n\nFix $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres; set $\\mathbb T^2_L:=\\mathbb R^2/(L_1\\mathbb Z\\times L_2\\mathbb Z)$. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\\mathbb T^2_L$, its lift is $\\widetilde f(\\widetilde x):=f([\\widetilde x])$ on $\\mathbb R^2$ and is periodic under each lattice translation $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$, $n_1,n_2\\in\\mathbb Z$. The notation $C^r$ for fields on $\\mathbb T^2_L\\times I$ or $\\mathbb T^2_L\\times[-h,0]\\times I$ means that the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with derivatives at $z=-h,0$ understood as continuous one-sided extensions. Horizontal coordinate partial derivatives are the corresponding derivatives of the periodic lift, so they are independent of the representative of a torus point. The flat reference liquid region is $\\Omega_0:=\\mathbb T^2_L\\times(-h,0)$; the bottom $z=-h$ is a fixed solid bed and the real first-order surface-displacement coefficient is $\\eta:\\mathbb T^2_L\\times I\\to\\mathbb R$, in metres. It is a formal perturbation coefficient, with no amplitude restriction such as $\\eta>-h$. For an optional finite-displacement geometric interpretation on a compact time interval $K\\subset I$, introduce a dimensionless $\\varepsilon>0$ and the graph $z=\\varepsilon\\eta(x,t)$. Continuity on the compact horizontal cell times $K$ bounds $|\\eta|$ by some finite $M$, so choosing $\\varepsilon M<h$ keeps that graph above the bed. This geometric scaling imposes no bound on the formal coefficient and asserts no nonlinear solution or approximation accuracy. Horizontal periodic faces are mathematical identifications, not physical walls.\n\nAdopt a homogeneous single-component liquid with constant mass density $\\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, constant downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and constant surface-tension coefficient $\\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre, equivalently kilograms per second squared. Here $\\rho$, $g$, $\\gamma$, and the constant gas pressure $p_a$ in pascals are primitive inputs of this formulation; $h,L_1,L_2$ are fixed geometric parameters. For the optional finite-displacement geometry on $K$, define $\\mathcal Q_{\\ell,\\varepsilon}:=\\{(x,z,t):x\\in\\mathbb T^2_L,\\ t\\in K,\\ -h<z<\\varepsilon\\eta(x,t)\\}$. If an auxiliary liquid-pressure field $p_{\\ell,\\varepsilon}:\\mathcal Q_{\\ell,\\varepsilon}\\to\\mathbb R$ in pascals is supplied, its liquid-side interface trace, when it exists, is $p_{\\ell,\\varepsilon}^\\Gamma(x,t):=\\lim_{z\\uparrow\\varepsilon\\eta(x,t)}p_{\\ell,\\varepsilon}(x,z,t)$. No extension or smoothness of this pressure across the interface is assumed. The gas is modeled only by the prescribed constant pressure $p_a$; no gas momentum equation is included. This optional geometric pressure is distinct from the formal first-order pressure coefficient used below. The reduced first-order model does not construct such a nonlinear pressure family and has no independent pressure evolution equation. Its independent fields are the unrestricted formal displacement coefficient $\\eta$ in metres and the scalar velocity-potential coefficient $\\phi$ in metres squared per second, both on the fixed reference geometry. Define the full Cartesian gradient by $\\nabla\\phi:=(\\partial_{x_1}\\phi,\\partial_{x_2}\\phi,\\partial_z\\phi)$ and the derived fluid-velocity vector field by $u:=\\nabla\\phi:\\mathbb T^2_L\\times[-h,0]\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^3$, in metres per second; there is no additive uniform velocity component. With $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, define $\\operatorname{div}u:=\\partial_{x_1}u_1+\\partial_{x_2}u_2+\\partial_z u_3$ and $\\operatorname{curl}u:=(\\partial_{x_2}u_3-\\partial_z u_2,\\partial_z u_1-\\partial_{x_1}u_3,\\partial_{x_1}u_2-\\partial_{x_2}u_1)$ using these Cartesian derivatives on the lifts. The model is inviscid, meaning no viscous-stress or viscous-dissipation terms are included; it is incompressible and irrotational, meaning $\\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\\operatorname{curl}u=0$. On the torus this potential assumption is stronger than irrotationality alone, since a curl-free field need not be the gradient of a periodic scalar. Assume $\\phi$ is at least $C^3$ and $\\eta$ is at least $C^2$ in the periodic-lift sense just defined; derivatives below are classical.\n\nSet $\\nabla_h:=(\\partial_{x_1},\\partial_{x_2})$ and $\\Delta_h:=\\partial_{x_1}^2+\\partial_{x_2}^2$ on the periodic lifts.
